reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors used a new method to conduct STM research on diamond and identified more than 40 defects as NV centers based on dI/dV conductance spectra. The density-of-states mapping of two-lobed wavefunctions aligned along the [111] crystallographic direction supports an anisotropic defect in diamond. However, in view of the following issues, we believe that the identification of NV is not definitive. The following issues need to be properly addressed before publication.
1. According to the “Sample preparation” part in methods, the NV depth is expected to be ~ 5 nm, while the STM topographies of NV- in fig.2, 3 and 4 all show a size smaller than 0.5 nm. This counterintuitively indicates an atomic spatial resolution with a tip-sample distance at the scale of 5 nm. Besides, the tunneling probability from the tip to the NV also needs an explanation, since it decays exponentially with an increasing distance and should be neglectable under such a distance.
2. In fig.2 f, the authors show a histogram from 45+ defects, counts from -1 eV to 0 eV are all classified into the ground state of NV-. Could the authors explain why the measured energy levels are so widely dispersed? P.S. the refs. of NV- and P1 energy levels (ref. 24, 25 and 26, 27) seem mislabeled.
3. In fig.3, the directionality of NV centers should be checked with more reliable methods. For example, polarized excitation laser can be used to identify the NV axis direction (refer to section IV of supplementary information of Nature Photonics 18, 230–235 (2024)).
4. In fig.4, the authors claim that NV centers’ charge state is manipulated. The straightest way to verify is to measure the photon counts before and after the manipulation (refer to NATURE COMMUNICATIONS 12, 2457 (2021)). It would really help to enhance the reliability of the identification of NV if such data are displayed.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The submitted article by Raghavan et al. presents a compelling study demonstrating atomic-scale imaging and charge-state manipulation of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) with a conductive graphene capping layer. By imaging the graphene–diamond heterostructure, the authors observe the characteristic honeycomb lattice of graphene and defect signatures attributed to sub-surface NV and P1 centers. These observations are supported by in-situ optical photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy. Using local differential conductance (dI/dV) spectroscopy, the authors could observe defects that exhibit signatures which can be attributed to NV⁻, as well as P1 centers. The authors also demonstrate the capability to image the two-lobed spatial structure of NV⁻ wavefunctions along the [111] crystallographic direction, and demonstrate tip-controlled charge-state switching from NV⁻ to NV⁰ using a positive sample bias.
The article is well written, and the method and results can be of high value to the scientific community. However, before recommending the article for publication, the following points should be addressed:
1. Tunneling Mechanism
The nature of the electronic coupling between the buried defects and the STM tip, mediated through the graphene layer, remains insufficiently explained. Specifically, the manuscript should clarify the nature of the tunnelling current observed in this study. Additionally, any role of band bending, interface dipoles, or charge transfer effects at the graphene–diamond interface should be discussed.
2. Depth Sensitivity and Lateral Resolution
A critical aspect of the study is the ability to detect sub-surface defects via STM. The authors should provide an estimate of the depth sensitivity of their method, i.e., the depth of the defects from which they expect a detectable dI/dV signal. Furthermore, the relationship between defect depth and lateral resolution should be addressed. Are there measurable trends in the apparent size or symmetry of the observed NV features (e.g., contrast, sharpness, lobe spacing) that correlate with defect depth? Such analysis should support the sub-surface origin of the features.
3. Role of Laser Illumination and the Laser-STM Setup
The authors mention, that the STM measurements were carried out in a newly developed laser-STM system. However, the importance of this system is not clearly stated. According to the sample preparation the utilized samples should have a homogeneous distribution of NV centers, so the in-situ PL measurements would not give any additional information on the presence of NV centers, compared with PL measurements outside of the STM. Furthermore, it is not stated in the manuscript, if laser-excitation of NV centers during the STM measurements is performed, and/or required for the described measurements. This should be clarified in the text. If laser excitation is used during spectroscopy, any effect of the illumination on the dI/dV spectra (e.g., peak shifts or intensity modulation) should be reported. Control experiments with and without laser illumination could provide important context for interpreting the tunnelling signals.
4. Defect Density and Statistical Analysis
The manuscript reports imaging of approximately 45 defects across two type-Ib diamond substrates, but lacks quantitative analysis of defect densities. The authors should provide the average areal densities for NV and P1 centers detected in STM. This should be compared with expected densities based on the utilized samples. Additionally, it would be informative to discuss the spatial distribution of defects, e.g., whether clustering is observed or whether the defects seem uniformly distributed.
5. Sample Set and Preparation Parameters
The authors state that three diamond samples were used, two nitrogen-rich type-Ib diamonds and one electronic-grade sample, but do not fully explain why two similar samples were required for the main experiments. More detail should be provided regarding the estimated NV and P1 concentrations in each sample, as derived from irradiation and annealing parameters, as well as supporting EPR or optical measurements.
Furthermore, the statements about the implantation energy, and depth of the electronic-grade crystal(s) are not very detailed. The authors should clarify the sample preparation method of these samples, as well as the motivation for choosing these parameters. Was the NV fluorescence of the electronic-grade sample also verified in-situ in the STM? If NV⁻ centers (even at lower density) were present optically but not detected in STM, this discrepancy deserves a more detailed discussion.
6. Tip-Induced Charge-State Control
The demonstration of bias-induced conversion between NV⁻ and NV⁰ should be better contextualized with respect to a similar previous study (Bian, K., et al., Nature Communications, 12(1), 1–9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-22709-9) which demonstrated reversable charge-state control of single NV centers using AFM tip gating. The authors should describe the unique aspects of their approach, and discuss how their observed charge-state dynamics compare to those prior results. Furthermore, they should elaborate on the choice of +5 V sample bias: was this empirically determined? Can a switching threshold voltage be defined? Has laser excitation been attempted to aid reverse the NV charge transition?
7. Comparison Between NV and P1 Defects
The manuscript would benefit from a direct comparison between the STM features attributed to NV centers and those assigned to P1 centers. What spatial topographies do the P1 centers exhibit, and how do they compare to the NVs two-lobed features?
8. Literature Context and Citations
The authors should be aware of a similar graphene-diamond heterostructure system, which has recently been demonstrated to show NV coherence enhancement, and should be referenced in their work (Hao, Y., et al., National Science Review, 12(5). https://doi.org/10.1093/NSR/NWAF076)
Conclusion and Recommendation
This manuscript presents important advances in atomic-scale imaging and charge-state control of quantum defects in diamond. However, to fully support its conclusions and improve clarity for a broad readership, the authors must address the above points through additional discussion, clarification, and where possible, supporting data. With these revisions, the study will be a valuable contribution to the fields of quantum sensing and scanning probe microscopy.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank reviewer #1 for thoroughly reviewing our manuscript and providing salient points for consideration. We answer each point in detail below.
1. According to the “Sample preparation” part in methods, the NV depth is expected to be ~ 5 nm, while the STM topographies of NV- in fig.2, 3 and 4 all show a size smaller than 0.5 nm. This counterintuitively indicates an atomic spatial resolution with a tip-sample distance at the scale of 5 nm. Besides, the tunneling probability from the tip to the NV also needs an explanation, since it decays exponentially with an increasing distance and should be neglectable under such a distance.
We would like to distinguish between the two types of samples discussed in our manuscript. One is type-1b and the other is electronic-grade sample. All the defects shown in Fig. 2-4 were measured in type-1b samples which have a relatively large density of NVs distributed uniformly throughout the sample, to the extent that it is reasonable to expect that there is a sizeable density of defects even within 1 nm of the surface in these type-1b samples.
The description of NV- depth of ~ 5 nm (mentioned by the reviewer above) is for the case for the other type of sample: electronic-grade. The electronic-grade sample has an extremely low density of natural defects. In this nearly NV-free sample, we applied 15N+ ion irradiation with the conditions which will implement N substitution at around 5 nm depth according to our SRIM simulations and the literature1–3. In contrast to the type-1b samples, we detect no defects in this irradiated electronic-grade sample (Fig. S9b), showing that the probing depth of our STM imaging is less than 5 nm.
Details clarifying the implantation parameters for the electronic-grade sample have now been added to the Methods section of the revised manuscript.
As for the expected depth at which defects can be probed with STM, literature shows this value to be approximately up to 2-2.5 nm. Here are a few examples aside from ones already discussed in the original manuscript, which we’ve discussed further in the revised manuscript in the newly added Supplementary Note 2:
• Nguyen, et al. (2018)4 use STM to study Se vacancy defects in the transition metal dichalcogenide PdSe up to 2 nm beneath the surface

• In another relevant work by Britnell, et al. (2012)7, electron tunneling through insulating layers of BN up to ~1.5 nm in thickness is examined

As there is almost no screening electron cloud near defects, how a defect below the surface appears in STM depends on the details of the wave function in the z-direction. Hence, one can often observe atomically resolved small lateral structure of sub-surface defects, as seen from the case of Ni defect at the CuO

In summary, the main type of samples used in our measurements were type-1b diamonds which are expected to have homogeneously distributed defects, including in the region from the surface to ~2.5 nm below the surface, which has been shown in the literature to be accessible by STM. Moreover, as is shown in the literature, the lateral resolution for the sub-surface defects in STM is not determined by distance from the surface for the case of insulators.

We agree that further clarification here would be useful. In the new version of the paper we show a comparison between the band edges at different areas of one of our type-1b samples ≈ 150 𝜇𝑚 apart in the Supplementary Information as Fig. S7. We also include it as Fig. R1 below. As can be seen, the band edges with respect to the Fermi energy can shift up to 0.5 eV or so in certain regions of the samples likely due to local potential variation in the sample. This kind of potential variation is often seen in low density of states materials like graphene and topological insulators. Our work, on the other hand, primarily uses type-1b diamond crystals with much higher defect densities. While the NVs in the previous works were ~200+ nm apart, the NVs in our work are less than 20 nm apart, at least an order of magnitude smaller in scale. This high density of NV- defects means that photon counts measurement from confocal microscopy cannot be done directly due to its spatial resolution limitation. This is the reason why we showed the charge state manipulation from atomic scale spectroscopy instead of confocal microscopy.
Nonetheless, for further verification of the charge state manipulation from the photon count, as suggested by the referee, we attempted to obtain PL at nm spatial resolution from tip-enhancement of the local laser electric field. Tip-enhanced PL (TEPL)15–18 is a technique which utilizes a nanocavity between a highly conductive tip and a highly conductive substrate, and is known to potentially allow for spatial resolution of < 10 nm. To this end, we approached a gold tip to the NVs in our type-1b diamond crystals. In new supplementary data added to the revised manuscript as Fig. S12 and displayed in Fig. R2 below, we find that the PL signal doesn’t change noticeably when the gold STM tip is on an NV defect, 50 nm away laterally, and withdrawn 500 nm away in Z from the sample. This is very likely due to the insulating nature of the diamond substrate which doesn’t allow to form an effective nanocavity with the tip for the local enhancement of PL. To make TEPL work, we would need a gold substrate and gold tip to form an effective nanocavity, and a sufficiently thin (≤ 5 nm) diamond membrane with NV centers which can sit in the nanocavity. Such fabrication techniques are not yet available but are the subject of ongoing research19.
In summary, despite technical limitations in being able to see a change in photon counts, we have been able to present consistent topographic and spectroscopic evidence for atomic-scale charge state manipulation. In addition, we have presented a platform which can enable measurements of contrast in photon counts from individual NVs with nm-resolution once the sample fabrication techniques evolve further in the coming years.

Given that the use of a monolayer graphene layer is an important component of our technique, we agree that further discussion would be useful, and we have now added the discussion and references below to the revised manuscript as Supplementary Note 1. In a few of these papers, density functional theory (DFT) modeling and calculations are performed to understand the nature of tunneling through graphene. For graphene on Cu as an example, Gonzalez-Herrero, et al. A similar reasoning may apply for tunneling through graphene into diamond defects, however given that ours is primarily an experimental work, we feel it would be more suitable to leave the theoretical modeling of this mechanism to future studies.
Regarding the effect of charge transfer, we note that Hao, et al. Their DFT works shows this depletion becomes effective for graphene-diamond distances less than 3-4 Å.

As there is almost no screening electron cloud near defects, how a defect below the surface appears in STM depends on the details of the wave function in the z-direction. For example, an STM study shows that the sub-surface defects in hBN from different layers only show difference in their spectral weight, not in their lateral size6.

The paper by Bian, et al. (2021)13 as well as a follow-up work by Zheng, et al. (2022)14 led by the same group of Prof. Ying Jiang at Peking University showcase a creative technique to achieve charge-state control of individual NV centers. While we referenced these works in our original manuscript, we’ve now included a further discussion in the revised manuscript as Supplementary Note 3 to distinguish our current work from the previous publications. These previous papers utilize an electronic-grade diamond substrate with extremely low NV center density such that confocal microscopy can be used and still see a change in photon counts when an individual NV charge state is manipulated.
Our work, which uses type-1b samples with significantly higher defect densities, distinguishes itself in several ways. One is that by using STM we can image the individual nitrogen-vacancy center wavefunction at the atomic scale for the first time. Secondly, while the NVs in the previous works were ~200+ nm apart, we show that it is possible to manipulate individual NVs which are less than 20 nm apart, an order of magnitude smaller in scale which is much below the spatial resolution limit of confocal microscopy identification of individual NVs. The higher defect density environment we work with helps us understand the effect of nearby defects and the spatial extent of charge state control in situations which are akin to those which may be encountered in technological applications.
Regarding the latter parts of this referee comment (“The choice of +5 V sample bias: was this empirically determined? Can a switching threshold voltage be defined?”), the choice of +5 V sample bias was determined empirically. We’ve found the threshold to be roughly above +2.5 V, however haven’t pursued finding an exact threshold value as it may also depend on the depth of the defect for example. The SPECS Nanonis SPM controller we use has voltage limits of -10 V to +10 V, but as shown in Fig. S14 of the revised manuscript, going close to 10 V can interact with and deform the graphene layer, so we used +5 V since it consistently allowed for charge state manipulation.
In addition, addressing the last part of this comment (“Has laser excitation been attempted to aid reverse the NV charge transition?”), we have also tried to use bias manipulation in the -/+ 5 V range with laser illumination to potentially aid in reversing the charge state transition. This configuration with laser illumination has similarities to the work by Bian, et al. (2021)13 and Zheng, et al. (2022)14, although those AFM-based works use much larger voltages above even 100 V. In our case, with the voltage ranges we use which are compatible with subsequent STM measurements, we don’t find an effect of the laser illumination in aiding reverse charge manipulation. We present this additional data in the revised manuscript as Fig. S15 and also display it in Fig. R8 below.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript presents a compelling study on the atomic-scale imaging and charge-state manipulation of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond using STM. The technique and the results, particularly the wavefunction mapping and local charge-state control, are of significant potential interest to the community. While I have one major concern regarding the evidence chain, I believe it can be adequately addressed through clarification in the text.
The most significant issue is that the spectroscopic identification of NV centers and their STM characterization are not performed on the same diamond sample.
Electronic-Grade Sample: As shown in Fig. 1, NV centers were created in this sample via ion implantation (~5 nm depth) and identified optically via their Zero-Phonon Line (ZPL). However, subsequent STM measurements on this sample did not detect any defect signals, which is consistent with the acknowledged STM probing depth limit of ~2.5 nm for defects in insulators.
Type-Ib Sample: The core STM data in Fig. 2-4 are acquired on high-nitrogen Type-Ib samples. The authors argue that the observed defects are NV centers based on their characteristic dI/dV spectra and two-lobed topography aligned with the [111] direction.
While this is not a loop-hole free validation, the authors provide a strong statistical argument. The combination of the STM data from over 40 defects with the ensemble photoluminescence from the Type-Ib samples makes a persuasive, population-level case for the source of the STM signals.
To prevent any potential misunderstanding and to accurately represent the nature of the evidence, the authors should explicitly state that the identification of the STM features as NV centers is based on a statistical correlation across a large defect population, rather than on a one-to-one, simultaneous optical and STM confirmation on the same defect. This clarification should be prominently placed in the Abstract and/or the main results summary to ensure readers have the correct context from the outset.
With the above clarification added, the manuscript will be significantly strengthened and suitable for publication. The methodological advance and the high-quality data presented are valuable contributions to the field.
Recommendation: Accept after Minor Revisions

The authors used a new method to conduct STM research on diamond and identified more than 40 defects as NV centers based on dI/dV conductance spectra. The density-of-states mapping of two-lobed wavefunctions aligned along the [111] crystallographic direction supports an anisotropic defect in diamond. However, in view of the following issues, we believe that the identification of NV is not definitive. The following issues need to be properly addressed before publication.
1. According to the “Sample preparation” part in methods, the NV depth is expected to be ~ 5 nm, while the STM topographies of NV- in fig.2, 3 and 4 all show a size smaller than 0.5 nm. This counterintuitively indicates an atomic spatial resolution with a tip-sample distance at the scale of 5 nm. Besides, the tunneling probability from the tip to the NV also needs an explanation, since it decays exponentially with an increasing distance and should be neglectable under such a distance.
2. In fig.2 f, the authors show a histogram from 45+ defects, counts from -1 eV to 0 eV are all classified into the ground state of NV-. Could the authors explain why the measured energy levels are so widely dispersed? P.S. the refs. of NV- and P1 energy levels (ref. 24, 25 and 26, 27) seem mislabeled.
3. In fig.3, the directionality of NV centers should be checked with more reliable methods. For example, polarized excitation laser can be used to identify the NV axis direction (refer to section IV of supplementary information of Nature Photonics 18, 230–235 (2024)).
4. In fig.4, the authors claim that NV centers’ charge state is manipulated. The straightest way to verify is to measure the photon counts before and after the manipulation (refer to NATURE COMMUNICATIONS 12, 2457 (2021)). It would really help to enhance the reliability of the identification of NV if such data are displayed.

### Reviewer 2

The submitted article by Raghavan et al. presents a compelling study demonstrating atomic-scale imaging and charge-state manipulation of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) with a conductive graphene capping layer. By imaging the graphene–diamond heterostructure, the authors observe the characteristic honeycomb lattice of graphene and defect signatures attributed to sub-surface NV and P1 centers. These observations are supported by in-situ optical photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy. Using local differential conductance (dI/dV) spectroscopy, the authors could observe defects that exhibit signatures which can be attributed to NV⁻, as well as P1 centers. The authors also demonstrate the capability to image the two-lobed spatial structure of NV⁻ wavefunctions along the [111] crystallographic direction, and demonstrate tip-controlled charge-state switching from NV⁻ to NV⁰ using a positive sample bias.
The article is well written, and the method and results can be of high value to the scientific community. However, before recommending the article for publication, the following points should be addressed:
1. Tunneling Mechanism
The nature of the electronic coupling between the buried defects and the STM tip, mediated through the graphene layer, remains insufficiently explained. Specifically, the manuscript should clarify the nature of the tunnelling current observed in this study. Additionally, any role of band bending, interface dipoles, or charge transfer effects at the graphene–diamond interface should be discussed.
2. Depth Sensitivity and Lateral Resolution
A critical aspect of the study is the ability to detect sub-surface defects via STM. The authors should provide an estimate of the depth sensitivity of their method, i.e., the depth of the defects from which they expect a detectable dI/dV signal. Furthermore, the relationship between defect depth and lateral resolution should be addressed. Are there measurable trends in the apparent size or symmetry of the observed NV features (e.g., contrast, sharpness, lobe spacing) that correlate with defect depth? Such analysis should support the sub-surface origin of the features.
3. Role of Laser Illumination and the Laser-STM Setup
The authors mention, that the STM measurements were carried out in a newly developed laser-STM system. However, the importance of this system is not clearly stated. According to the sample preparation the utilized samples should have a homogeneous distribution of NV centers, so the in-situ PL measurements would not give any additional information on the presence of NV centers, compared with PL measurements outside of the STM. Furthermore, it is not stated in the manuscript, if laser-excitation of NV centers during the STM measurements is performed, and/or required for the described measurements. This should be clarified in the text. If laser excitation is used during spectroscopy, any effect of the illumination on the dI/dV spectra (e.g., peak shifts or intensity modulation) should be reported. Control experiments with and without laser illumination could provide important context for interpreting the tunnelling signals.
4. Defect Density and Statistical Analysis
The manuscript reports imaging of approximately 45 defects across two type-Ib diamond substrates, but lacks quantitative analysis of defect densities. The authors should provide the average areal densities for NV and P1 centers detected in STM. This should be compared with expected densities based on the utilized samples. Additionally, it would be informative to discuss the spatial distribution of defects, e.g., whether clustering is observed or whether the defects seem uniformly distributed.
5. Sample Set and Preparation Parameters
The authors state that three diamond samples were used, two nitrogen-rich type-Ib diamonds and one electronic-grade sample, but do not fully explain why two similar samples were required for the main experiments. More detail should be provided regarding the estimated NV and P1 concentrations in each sample, as derived from irradiation and annealing parameters, as well as supporting EPR or optical measurements.
Furthermore, the statements about the implantation energy, and depth of the electronic-grade crystal(s) are not very detailed. The authors should clarify the sample preparation method of these samples, as well as the motivation for choosing these parameters. Was the NV fluorescence of the electronic-grade sample also verified in-situ in the STM? If NV⁻ centers (even at lower density) were present optically but not detected in STM, this discrepancy deserves a more detailed discussion.
6. Tip-Induced Charge-State Control
The demonstration of bias-induced conversion between NV⁻ and NV⁰ should be better contextualized with respect to a similar previous study (Bian, K., et al., Nature Communications, 12(1), 1–9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-22709-9) which demonstrated reversable charge-state control of single NV centers using AFM tip gating. The authors should describe the unique aspects of their approach, and discuss how their observed charge-state dynamics compare to those prior results. Furthermore, they should elaborate on the choice of +5 V sample bias: was this empirically determined? Can a switching threshold voltage be defined? Has laser excitation been attempted to aid reverse the NV charge transition?
7. Comparison Between NV and P1 Defects
The manuscript would benefit from a direct comparison between the STM features attributed to NV centers and those assigned to P1 centers. What spatial topographies do the P1 centers exhibit, and how do they compare to the NVs two-lobed features?
8. Literature Context and Citations
The authors should be aware of a similar graphene-diamond heterostructure system, which has recently been demonstrated to show NV coherence enhancement, and should be referenced in their work (Hao, Y., et al., National Science Review, 12(5). https://doi.org/10.1093/NSR/NWAF076)
Conclusion and Recommendation
This manuscript presents important advances in atomic-scale imaging and charge-state control of quantum defects in diamond. However, to fully support its conclusions and improve clarity for a broad readership, the authors must address the above points through additional discussion, clarification, and where possible, supporting data. With these revisions, the study will be a valuable contribution to the fields of quantum sensing and scanning probe microscopy.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The authors used a new method to conduct STM research on diamond and identified more than 40 defects as NV centers based on dI/dV conductance spectra. The density-of-states mapping of two-lobed wavefunctions aligned along the [111] crystallographic direction supports an anisotropic defect in diamond. However, in view of the following issues, we believe that the identification of NV is not definitive. The following issues need to be properly addressed before publication.
1. According to the “Sample preparation” part in methods, the NV depth is expected to be ~ 5 nm, while the STM topographies of NV- in fig.2, 3 and 4 all show a size smaller than 0.5 nm. This counterintuitively indicates an atomic spatial resolution with a tip-sample distance at the scale of 5 nm. Besides, the tunneling probability from the tip to the NV also needs an explanation, since it decays exponentially with an increasing distance and should be neglectable under such a distance.
2. In fig.2 f, the authors show a histogram from 45+ defects, counts from -1 eV to 0 eV are all classified into the ground state of NV-. Could the authors explain why the measured energy levels are so widely dispersed? P.S. the refs. of NV- and P1 energy levels (ref. 24, 25 and 26, 27) seem mislabeled.
3. In fig.3, the directionality of NV centers should be checked with more reliable methods. For example, polarized excitation laser can be used to identify the NV axis direction (refer to section IV of supplementary information of Nature Photonics 18, 230–235 (2024)).
4. In fig.4, the authors claim that NV centers’ charge state is manipulated. The straightest way to verify is to measure the photon counts before and after the manipulation (refer to NATURE COMMUNICATIONS 12, 2457 (2021)). It would really help to enhance the reliability of the identification of NV if such data are displayed.

### Reviewer 2

The submitted article by Raghavan et al. presents a compelling study demonstrating atomic-scale imaging and charge-state manipulation of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) with a conductive graphene capping layer. By imaging the graphene–diamond heterostructure, the authors observe the characteristic honeycomb lattice of graphene and defect signatures attributed to sub-surface NV and P1 centers. These observations are supported by in-situ optical photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy. Using local differential conductance (dI/dV) spectroscopy, the authors could observe defects that exhibit signatures which can be attributed to NV⁻, as well as P1 centers. The authors also demonstrate the capability to image the two-lobed spatial structure of NV⁻ wavefunctions along the [111] crystallographic direction, and demonstrate tip-controlled charge-state switching from NV⁻ to NV⁰ using a positive sample bias.
The article is well written, and the method and results can be of high value to the scientific community. However, before recommending the article for publication, the following points should be addressed:
1. Tunneling Mechanism
The nature of the electronic coupling between the buried defects and the STM tip, mediated through the graphene layer, remains insufficiently explained. Specifically, the manuscript should clarify the nature of the tunnelling current observed in this study. Additionally, any role of band bending, interface dipoles, or charge transfer effects at the graphene–diamond interface should be discussed.
2. Depth Sensitivity and Lateral Resolution
A critical aspect of the study is the ability to detect sub-surface defects via STM. The authors should provide an estimate of the depth sensitivity of their method, i.e., the depth of the defects from which they expect a detectable dI/dV signal. Furthermore, the relationship between defect depth and lateral resolution should be addressed. Are there measurable trends in the apparent size or symmetry of the observed NV features (e.g., contrast, sharpness, lobe spacing) that correlate with defect depth? Such analysis should support the sub-surface origin of the features.
3. Role of Laser Illumination and the Laser-STM Setup
The authors mention, that the STM measurements were carried out in a newly developed laser-STM system. However, the importance of this system is not clearly stated. According to the sample preparation the utilized samples should have a homogeneous distribution of NV centers, so the in-situ PL measurements would not give any additional information on the presence of NV centers, compared with PL measurements outside of the STM. Furthermore, it is not stated in the manuscript, if laser-excitation of NV centers during the STM measurements is performed, and/or required for the described measurements. This should be clarified in the text. If laser excitation is used during spectroscopy, any effect of the illumination on the dI/dV spectra (e.g., peak shifts or intensity modulation) should be reported. Control experiments with and without laser illumination could provide important context for interpreting the tunnelling signals.
4. Defect Density and Statistical Analysis
The manuscript reports imaging of approximately 45 defects across two type-Ib diamond substrates, but lacks quantitative analysis of defect densities. The authors should clarify the sample preparation method of these samples, as well as the motivation for choosing these parameters. 8. Literature Context and Citations
The authors should be aware of a similar graphene-diamond heterostructure system, which has recently been demonstrated to show NV coherence enhancement, and should be referenced in their work (Hao, Y., et al., National Science Review, 12(5). https://doi.org/10.1093/NSR/NWAF076)
Conclusion and Recommendation
This manuscript presents important advances in atomic-scale imaging and charge-state control of quantum defects in diamond. However, to fully support its conclusions and improve clarity for a broad readership, the authors must address the above points through additional discussion, clarification, and where possible, supporting data. With these revisions, the study will be a valuable contribution to the fields of quantum sensing and scanning probe microscopy.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The authors used a new method to conduct STM research on diamond and identified more than 40 defects as NV centers based on dI/dV conductance spectra. The density-of-states mapping of two-lobed wavefunctions aligned along the [111] crystallographic direction supports an anisotropic defect in diamond. However, in view of the following issues, we believe that the identification of NV is not definitive. The following issues need to be properly addressed before publication.
1. According to the “Sample preparation” part in methods, the NV depth is expected to be ~ 5 nm, while the STM topographies of NV- in fig.2, 3 and 4 all show a size smaller than 0.5 nm. This counterintuitively indicates an atomic spatial resolution with a tip-sample distance at the scale of 5 nm. Besides, the tunneling probability from the tip to the NV also needs an explanation, since it decays exponentially with an increasing distance and should be neglectable under such a distance.
2. In fig.2 f, the authors show a histogram from 45+ defects, counts from -1 eV to 0 eV are all classified into the ground state of NV-. Could the authors explain why the measured energy levels are so widely dispersed? P.S. the refs. of NV- and P1 energy levels (ref. 24, 25 and 26, 27) seem mislabeled.
3. In fig.3, the directionality of NV centers should be checked with more reliable methods. For example, polarized excitation laser can be used to identify the NV axis direction (refer to section IV of supplementary information of Nature Photonics 18, 230–235 (2024)).
4. In fig.4, the authors claim that NV centers’ charge state is manipulated. The straightest way to verify is to measure the photon counts before and after the manipulation (refer to NATURE COMMUNICATIONS 12, 2457 (2021)). It would really help to enhance the reliability of the identification of NV if such data are displayed.

### Reviewer 2

The submitted article by Raghavan et al. presents a compelling study demonstrating atomic-scale imaging and charge-state manipulation of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) with a conductive graphene capping layer. By imaging the graphene–diamond heterostructure, the authors observe the characteristic honeycomb lattice of graphene and defect signatures attributed to sub-surface NV and P1 centers. These observations are supported by in-situ optical photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy. Using local differential conductance (dI/dV) spectroscopy, the authors could observe defects that exhibit signatures which can be attributed to NV⁻, as well as P1 centers. The authors also demonstrate the capability to image the two-lobed spatial structure of NV⁻ wavefunctions along the [111] crystallographic direction, and demonstrate tip-controlled charge-state switching from NV⁻ to NV⁰ using a positive sample bias.
The article is well written, and the method and results can be of high value to the scientific community. However, before recommending the article for publication, the following points should be addressed:
1. Tunneling Mechanism
The nature of the electronic coupling between the buried defects and the STM tip, mediated through the graphene layer, remains insufficiently explained. Specifically, the manuscript should clarify the nature of the tunnelling current observed in this study. Additionally, any role of band bending, interface dipoles, or charge transfer effects at the graphene–diamond interface should be discussed.
2. Depth Sensitivity and Lateral Resolution
A critical aspect of the study is the ability to detect sub-surface defects via STM. The authors should provide an estimate of the depth sensitivity of their method, i.e., the depth of the defects from which they expect a detectable dI/dV signal. Furthermore, the relationship between defect depth and lateral resolution should be addressed. Are there measurable trends in the apparent size or symmetry of the observed NV features (e.g., contrast, sharpness, lobe spacing) that correlate with defect depth? Such analysis should support the sub-surface origin of the features.
3. Role of Laser Illumination and the Laser-STM Setup
The authors mention, that the STM measurements were carried out in a newly developed laser-STM system. However, the importance of this system is not clearly stated. According to the sample preparation the utilized samples should have a homogeneous distribution of NV centers, so the in-situ PL measurements would not give any additional information on the presence of NV centers, compared with PL measurements outside of the STM. Furthermore, it is not stated in the manuscript, if laser-excitation of NV centers during the STM measurements is performed, and/or required for the described measurements. This should be clarified in the text. If laser excitation is used during spectroscopy, any effect of the illumination on the dI/dV spectra (e.g., peak shifts or intensity modulation) should be reported. Control experiments with and without laser illumination could provide important context for interpreting the tunnelling signals.
4. Defect Density and Statistical Analysis
The manuscript reports imaging of approximately 45 defects across two type-Ib diamond substrates, but lacks quantitative analysis of defect densities. The authors should provide the average areal densities for NV and P1 centers detected in STM. This should be compared with expected densities based on the utilized samples. Additionally, it would be informative to discuss the spatial distribution of defects, e.g., whether clustering is observed or whether the defects seem uniformly distributed.
5. Sample Set and Preparation Parameters
The authors state that three diamond samples were used, two nitrogen-rich type-Ib diamonds and one electronic-grade sample, but do not fully explain why two similar samples were required for the main experiments. More detail should be provided regarding the estimated NV and P1 concentrations in each sample, as derived from irradiation and annealing parameters, as well as supporting EPR or optical measurements.
Furthermore, the statements about the implantation energy, and depth of the electronic-grade crystal(s) are not very detailed. The authors should clarify the sample preparation method of these samples, as well as the motivation for choosing these parameters. Was the NV fluorescence of the electronic-grade sample also verified in-situ in the STM? If NV⁻ centers (even at lower density) were present optically but not detected in STM, this discrepancy deserves a more detailed discussion.
6. Tip-Induced Charge-State Control
The demonstration of bias-induced conversion between NV⁻ and NV⁰ should be better contextualized with respect to a similar previous study (Bian, K., et al., Nature Communications, 12(1), 1–9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-22709-9) which demonstrated reversable charge-state control of single NV centers using AFM tip gating. The authors should describe the unique aspects of their approach, and discuss how their observed charge-state dynamics compare to those prior results. Furthermore, they should elaborate on the choice of +5 V sample bias: was this empirically determined? Can a switching threshold voltage be defined? Has laser excitation been attempted to aid reverse the NV charge transition?
7. Comparison Between NV and P1 Defects
The manuscript would benefit from a direct comparison between the STM features attributed to NV centers and those assigned to P1 centers. What spatial topographies do the P1 centers exhibit, and how do they compare to the NVs two-lobed features?
8. Literature Context and Citations
The authors should be aware of a similar graphene-diamond heterostructure system, which has recently been demonstrated to show NV coherence enhancement, and should be referenced in their work (Hao, Y., et al., National Science Review, 12(5). https://doi.org/10.1093/NSR/NWAF076)
Conclusion and Recommendation
This manuscript presents important advances in atomic-scale imaging and charge-state control of quantum defects in diamond. However, to fully support its conclusions and improve clarity for a broad readership, the authors must address the above points through additional discussion, clarification, and where possible, supporting data. With these revisions, the study will be a valuable contribution to the fields of quantum sensing and scanning probe microscopy.

6. Tip-Induced Charge-State Control
The paper by Bian, et al. (2021)13 as well as a follow-up work by Zheng, et al. (2022)14 led by the same group of Prof. Ying Jiang at Peking University showcase a creative technique to achieve charge-state control of individual NV centers. While we referenced these works in our original manuscript, we’ve now included a further discussion in the revised manuscript as Supplementary Note 3 to distinguish our current work from the previous publications. These previous papers utilize an electronic-grade diamond substrate with extremely low NV center density such that confocal microscopy can be used and still see a change in photon counts when an individual NV charge state is manipulated.
Our work, which uses type-1b samples with significantly higher defect densities, distinguishes itself in several ways. One is that by using STM we can image the individual nitrogen-vacancy center wavefunction at the atomic scale for the first time. Secondly, while the NVs in the previous works were ~200+ nm apart, we show that it is possible to manipulate individual NVs which are less than 20 nm apart, an order of magnitude smaller in scale which is much below the spatial resolution limit of confocal microscopy identification of individual NVs. The higher defect density environment we work with helps us understand the effect of nearby defects and the spatial extent of charge state control in situations which are akin to those which may be encountered in technological applications.
Regarding the latter parts of this referee comment (“The choice of +5 V sample bias: was this empirically determined? Can a switching threshold voltage be defined?”), the choice of +5 V sample bias was determined empirically. We’ve found the threshold to be roughly above +2.5 V, however haven’t pursued finding an exact threshold value as it may also depend on the depth of the defect for example. The SPECS Nanonis SPM controller we use has voltage limits of -10 V to +10 V, but as shown in Fig. S14 of the revised manuscript, going close to 10 V can interact with and deform the graphene layer, so we used +5 V since it consistently allowed for charge state manipulation.
In addition, addressing the last part of this comment (“Has laser excitation been attempted to aid reverse the NV charge transition?”), we have also tried to use bias manipulation in the -/+ 5 V range with laser illumination to potentially aid in reversing the charge state transition. This configuration with laser illumination has similarities to the work by Bian, et al. (2021)13 and Zheng, et al. (2022)14, although those AFM-based works use much larger voltages above even 100 V. In our case, with the voltage ranges we use which are compatible with subsequent STM measurements, we don’t find an effect of the laser illumination in aiding reverse charge manipulation. We present this additional data in the revised manuscript as Fig. S15 and also display it in Fig. R8 below.
